details:
**"A Good Man Is Hard to Find"**
O'Connor's most famous short story (1953), and the most common title clue for her. A Georgia family sets off on a road trip to Florida, has a car accident on a back road, and is murdered by an escaped convict called the Misfit. The title phrase is spoken by the restaurant owner Red Sammy.

**The Misfit and the Grandmother**
The escaped criminal and the selfish, manipulative Grandmother at the center of "A Good Man Is Hard to Find." His henchmen Hiram and Bobby Lee take the family into the woods and shoot them. The Grandmother has a moment of grace, reaching out and saying "Why you're one of my babies. You're one of my own children!", and the Misfit recoils and shoots her. He then says "She would of been a good woman, if it had been somebody there to shoot her every minute of her life," and "Shut up, Bobby Lee. It's no real pleasure in life."

**Pitty Sing and the house with the secret panel**
In "A Good Man Is Hard to Find," the Grandmother tells her grandchildren John Wesley and June Star about an old plantation house near Toombsboro with a secret panel, so their father Bailey agrees to detour down a dirt road. She then realizes the house is actually in Tennessee, startles, and upsets the basket hiding her cat, Pitty Sing. The cat jumps onto Bailey's shoulder and causes the crash.

**Red Sammy Butts and The Tower**
The family stops at The Tower, a barbecue restaurant run by Red Sammy Butts, where a gray monkey is chained to a chinaberry tree. Red Sammy and the Grandmother agree that "a good man is hard to find" these days. The Misfit also says Jesus "thrown everything off balance" and that no one ever gave the undertaker a tip.

**"Good Country People" and Hulga's wooden leg**
Joy Hopewell is a 32-year-old with a PhD in philosophy who has an artificial leg. She legally renamed herself "Hulga," a name that makes her mother think of the broad blank hull of a battleship. She plans to seduce a naive young Bible salesman in a hayloft, but he steals her prosthetic leg and leaves her stranded.

**Manley Pointer**
The fake Bible salesman of "Good Country People," whom Mrs. Hopewell takes for "good country people" and the "salt of the earth." In the hayloft he opens a hollow Bible containing a flask of whiskey, a deck of obscene playing cards, and condoms. He sneers, "I been believing in nothing ever since I was born!" Hulga quotes the philosopher Malebranche ("We are not our own light!"), and her mother keeps repeating platitudes like "Nothing is perfect" and "that's life."

**"Everything That Rises Must Converge"**
The title story of O'Connor's posthumous 1965 collection, taking its title from a phrase of the Jesuit thinker Pierre Teilhard de Chardin. The liberal, resentful Julian escorts his racist mother on a newly desegregated bus to her weight-reducing class at the Y, which she attends for her high blood pressure. She boasts of her ancestors the Godhighs and a grandfather with "a plantation and two hundred slaves." While she tries on her hat, Julian waits like Saint Sebastian waiting for the arrows. On the bus he asks a Black man for a match before noticing a No Smoking sign.

**The hideous hat and Carver's penny**
In "Everything That Rises Must Converge," Julian's mother wears an ugly green-and-purple velvet hat, and a Black woman on the bus wears the identical hat. When Julian's mother condescendingly offers the woman's little son Carver a "bright new penny," the woman knocks her down. Julian's mother then suffers a stroke and dies at the bus stop.

**"The Life You Save May Be Your Own"**
A drifter, the one-armed Tom T. Shiftlet, arrives at the farm of the old woman Lucynell Crater, fixes her old car (a 1928 or 1929 Ford), and marries her deaf-mute daughter, also named Lucynell. He abandons the daughter asleep at a diner on their honeymoon. Driving toward Mobile, he picks up a hitchhiker, passes the title highway-safety slogan on a billboard, and then drives into a rainstorm.

**"The River"**
A young boy, Harry Ashfield, is taken by his babysitter Mrs. Connin to a riverside baptism by the preacher Bevel Summers, and he says his own name is Bevel. Returning to the river alone to find the Kingdom of Christ, he drowns while the menacing Mr. Paradise tries to grab him.

**Wise Blood**
O'Connor's first novel (1952). The war veteran Hazel Motes returns from the army to his home region in Tennessee and preaches the "Church Without Christ." The zookeeper Enoch Emery steals a shrunken mummy from a museum to serve as its "new jesus."

**The Violent Bear It Away**
O'Connor's second and final novel (1960). The teenage Francis Marion Tarwater is raised by his fanatical great-uncle to be a prophet and resists, then accepts, the call to baptize his cousin.

**"Revelation"**
In a doctor's waiting room, the self-satisfied Ruby Turpin is hit with a book called Human Development by a college girl named Mary Grace, who calls her an "old wart hog" from hell. Back at her farm, while hosing down her "pig parlor," Ruby has a vision of souls ascending to heaven.

**"Parker's Back" and "Greenleaf"**
In "Parker's Back," the Navy veteran O. E. Parker gets a tattoo of the Byzantine Christ on his back, but his fundamentalist wife Sarah Ruth calls it idolatry, beats him, and throws him out. In "Greenleaf," the farm owner Mrs. May is gored by a stray bull that her hired man Mr. Greenleaf was slow to shoot.

**"A Late Encounter with the Enemy," "The Displaced Person," and other stories**
In "A Late Encounter with the Enemy," a 104-year-old Confederate "general" dies onstage in his wheelchair at his granddaughter Sally Poker Sash's graduation, after earlier ranting about "pretty guls." In "The Displaced Person," the Polish refugee Mr. Guizac is killed by a rolling tractor while the farm's people watch. Other stories include "A Circle in the Fire" (boys led by Powell Boyd set Mrs. Cope's woods on fire) and "The Geranium." O'Connor was a devout Catholic Southern Gothic writer from Georgia who died of lupus in 1964.
